name: Cannon
lede: Cannon is a very dark, slightly green-tinted grey, near gunmetal; its name is undocumented in the books.

sections.title: What the books say
sections.body:
No color book here describes a cannon color. Cannon appear only in passing: Spanish ships were stripped of timber, iron and cannon once they reached the New World [1], and Perkin's madder works dropped cannon balls into a rotating cylinder to help mix the dye bath [2].

One pigment trace is real: terra di campana was said to be earth from the crust that formed on the moulds used to cast bells and cannon [3]. The origin of this swatch name is undocumented, and it sits nearest to [[gunmetal]], [[charcoal]] and [[black]], with [[bramble]] close by in darkness.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Dark greys are everywhere in paint. Cannon appears in 5.78% of the 23,781 paintings in our archive (1,374 paintings, as photographed), more often than 91% of named colors [4]. It peaks in the 1700s, at 1.5 times the rate expected from the baseline [4].

notes.cite: ColorHub archive, 23,781 museum paintings as photographed (data/graph/fieldnotes, CIEDE2000)

questions.q: In which decade does cannon peak in our painting archive?
True or false: the books document where this color name comes from.

openers: Dark grey is common in museum paintings: cannon appears in nearly 6% of them.
